metadata.title: Huntingdonshire teenager becomes country's youngest bookmaker at 18
metadata.contentSnippet: A Huntingdonshire teenager has swapped plumbing training to become the country's youngest bookmaker.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdonshire teenager becomes country's youngest bookmaker at 18
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire teenager has swapped plumbing training to become the country's youngest bookmaker. Archie Bailey, 18, from Hartford has joined his proud dad Steve in working as an on-course bookmaker at racecourses across the country. He joined Steve within days of turning 18 earlier this summer. Steve lives in Peterborough and previously ran an estate agency in March. Archie Bailey loves working alongside his dad Steve on racecourses across the country. (Image: Marilyn Bailey) The father and son trade under the name of Stevie Stretch. Archie's mum, Marilyn also from Hartford, said her son had been doing a plumbing apprenticeship, but decided it was not for him, and instead decided to join his dad in the paddock. The teenager has always had an interest in betting and felt the move into the industry was the natural step to take so he could help grow the family business while testing his own skills of the betting market. Archie Bailey has become the country's youngest bookie. (Image: Marilyn Bailey) Archie has already shown he can read the betting markets and hopes to gain experience alongside other bookmakers before taking the family business forward. Bookmaking has also become something of a family tradition, with Steve’s 91-year-old father previously accompanying him to racecourses and working alongside him on pitches. Marilyn said Steve is delighted to have their son working alongside him now his own father is unable to attend meetings. Archie Bailey loves working alongside his dad Steve on racecourses across the country. (Image: Marilyn Bailey) Alongside his work with his father, Archie works as an introducing broker for a day trading company specialising in gold. Marilyn said he is also keen to broaden his experience by working for other bookmakers.

metadata.title: Undercover female officers run county's streets in crackdown on harassment
metadata.contentSnippet: Police are targeting parts of Cambridgeshire after more than three-quarters of women in a survey said they had felt unsafe while running.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Undercover female officers run county's streets in crackdown on harassment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police are targeting parts of Cambridgeshire after more than three-quarters of women in a survey said they had felt unsafe while running. Cambridgeshire Constabulary’s Operation Vexa is focused on preventing harassment and other offending in public spaces, with activity being directed towards locations where women reported experiencing problems. The first undercover operation was held in Huntingdon on Monday night when a group of female officers ran a circuit around the town, including Hinchingbrooke Park, which was one of the areas highlighted in the survey. Det Supt Dave Taylor gives his team a briefing before the first night of action in Huntingdon as part of Operation Vexa aimed at improving women's safety. (Image: Sarah Cliss) They were backed up by male officers in uniform in vehicles ready to act if the need arose during the hour-long exercise. The women completed their run without incident, but runner Det Supt Denise Harper said many women do not enjoy the same freedom. "When I was asked about this operation, I volunteered to do it straight away. I feel very passionately about keeping women and girls safe," she said. "It's not right that women and girls have to put certain measures in place, and think about their personal safety when they are trying to go about normal activities like exercising and running." Before the women took to their heels on the 3.2 mile circuitous run, they and their male colleagues were given a pre-operation briefing by Det Supt Dave Taylor, who is the leading officer responsible for protecting vulnerable people for Cambridgeshire. He explained to the team, alongside representatives from the media, the importance of Operation Vexa, which this week will see two further exercises in Cambridge and Peterborough. He said the operation aimed to prevent and tackle offending by identifying perpetrators before their behaviour escalates. Two of the female officers who ran the streets of Huntingdon in the first of three nights of action as part of Operation Vexa. (Image: Sarah Cliss) He said 2,149 women had responded to a public survey conducted in August with more than three-quarters saying they felt unsafe while running. Only three per cent had reported their concerns to police, he said. Det Supt Taylor said: "That means just because it is not being reported, it is not happening. I am hoping this operation will increase women's confidence reporting offences to the police." More than half, 54 per cent of those who took part in the survey, said they had experienced harassment and 64 per cent said they had been cat-called. Det Supt Denise Harper was among the women runners. She said she felt passionately about trying to improve the safety of women and girls on Cambridgeshire's streets. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The team will carry out a similar operation along Cambridge’s riverside corridor on Wednesday before moving to Peterborough on Friday. Det Supt Taylor said early evening and the hours after dark were key deployment times. But he warned that harassment can happen in daylight and that a lack of recorded incidents does not mean there is no risk. Det Supt Taylor said women’s experiences had shaped the operation. He said: “We are listening to runners’ experiences and using them for targeted prevention activity. “These operations are being carried out in areas where women who responded to the survey told us they have experienced problems. “Through this operation we want to target poor behaviour and criminal offences to enable women to be and feel safer in public spaces.” He described Operation Vexa as a “perpetrator-focused prevention and enforcement activity in public spaces”. The operation aims to prevent harm, deter harassment, identify repeat or escalating behaviour and intervene when offences or risks require police action. Officers will also use the deployments to build intelligence about concerning behaviour, people, vehicles, locations and times, while Det Supt Taylor emphasised the force takes women's safety seriously, and wants to increase their confidence that reports of harassment and sexualised behaviour will be taken seriously. The briefing listed possible incidents, including sexualised comments, gestures or approaches, being followed on foot, by bicycle, e-scooter or vehicle, stalking, assault and threatened violence. The plain-clothes officers were to report concerning behaviour, locations and risks while following agreed routes and staying in contact with colleagues throughout the run. Uniformed male officers were there to intervene if needed to safeguard people, make an arrest or preserve evidence. The force said its aim is to make Cambridgeshire’s public spaces safer by preventing harm where women have reported harassment or fear. Det Supt Taylor said women should not have to change where, when or how they exercise because they fear harassment. The operation also draws on the Angiolini Inquiry, which found that women routinely change their routes, plans and behaviour because of safety fears. The briefing said offences and concerning behaviour in public spaces can go unreported and unrecorded. It says non-contact and early-stage sexual behaviour should be taken seriously because it may be part of a pattern that repeats or escalates. Operation Vexa is part of the constabulary’s wider response to violence against women and girls. It aims to prevent offending and change perpetrators’ behaviour instead of asking women to change their routines.

metadata.title: DWP Winter Fuel Payment warning as pensioners say they have to wrap up in blankets
metadata.contentSnippet: Many fear they will be forced to sit in freezing homes and wrap themselves in blankets this winter as household energy bills are set to jump by 26% in January.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP Winter Fuel Payment warning as pensioners say they have to wrap up in blankets
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Pensioners fear they will be forced to sit in freezing homes and wrap themselves in blankets this winter as household energy bills are set to jump by 26% in January. Charities have warned the price rise could leave older people struggling to afford to heat their homes - despite DWP winter fuel payments - while terminally ill people face the added worry of keeping vital medical equipment running and maintaining a warm environment. Age UK and palliative care charity Sue Ryder have both called for targeted energy support for those most at risk as the cost of keeping warm rises. One in five pensioner households in Great Britain are likely to be in “fuel stress” this winter, Age UK explained of its analysis. This means they will spend more than 10% of their after-tax household income on energy bills. Among the poorest households – those in the bottom 20% of the income distribution – almost half are expected to be in this position. The charity estimates the average pensioner household will spend £1 in every £14 of its income on gas and electricity at the forecast prices. Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, said the latest increase “will be deeply worrying for many older people who are already anxious about how they will afford to keep warm this winter”. While welcoming the Government's £100 energy payment for households from January, and winter fuel payments more broadly, she warned it was “simply not enough”. She added: “Another increase in energy bills risks pushing more households into hardship at a time when keeping warm is not a luxury, but an essential part of protecting their health. “Our recent analysis suggests that this winter is set to be extremely challenging for pensioners who are struggling to afford the energy they need. That’s why we believe ministers should introduce an emergency energy support package targeted at those households most at risk of cold homes, financial hardship and worsening health this winter.” Three pensioners in their 80s have spoken about the difficult choices they fear they will face as bills rise. Roger, who did not give his surname, described the 26% increase as “unbelievable” and said it “will lead to utter despair” for many older people. He works in a care home and said he can still “balance the books”, but added: “It worries me what might happen if I’m unable to work one day”. Sheila, who also did not give her surname, said she had not used her central heating for years and instead relied on a couple of electric heaters in whichever room she was in. She said that on particularly cold nights she was “often left sitting in a cold house, wrapping myself up in blankets”. Age UK is encouraging older people on low incomes who are struggling with their bills to contact its free advice line on 0800 169 65 65 or visit www.ageuk.org.uk/money . The rise in energy costs could also have serious consequences for people living with terminal illnesses, Sue Ryder warned. Dr Paul Perkins, the charity's chief medical director, said the increase could “darken the precious time they have left”. Recommended reading: He said: “It may make them anxious and afraid, wondering how they’re going to keep themselves warm and keep their medical equipment going when they should be spending time making memories with loved ones. “Many rely on higher levels of heating to stop symptoms worsening, while others depend on vital electrical medical equipment, which in some cases is keeping them alive. All this leaves them with significantly increased costs. “Targeted help with energy costs would remove a substantial burden and allow people to make the most of the time they have left, not spending it watching their bank balance. Everyone deserves to live well and with dignity until the very end.” Tomorrow morning, Ofgem will announce the Jan-March energy price cap. It's likely to go up 26% but what after that? And does this mean you should fix? A clip from my Martin Lewis Money Show energy special tonight. Watch the full thing for far more help: https://t.co/Vcrj5Jywiw https://t.co/yR2mlzgyBw — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 24, 2026 Becca Stacey, from end-of-life care charity Marie Curie, said: “No energy support scheme specifically targets people living with terminal illness, despite extensive evidence of higher bills and significant financial hardship at the end of life.” She said support available through the £100 household energy payment, £150 Warm Home Discount and £300 Winter Fuel Payment “covers just a quarter of an average household’s energy bills”. Marie Curie is calling for a 50% energy social tariff for people living with a terminal illness. The charity said its modelling suggests this could lift up to 54,000 people – 45% of those dying – out of fuel poverty. Have you turned your heating on yet? Tell us in the comments below...

metadata.title: 10 commonly misunderstood UK road signs - how many can you recognise?
metadata.contentSnippet: Understand ten road signs, including no vehicles, toad crossings, clearways and pass either side.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 commonly misunderstood UK road signs - how many can you recognise?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A blank red-ringed road sign bans vehicles, including bicycles unless they are being pushed. It is one of several signs whose meaning might not be immediately obvious to drivers. The Department for Transport groups traffic signs into three basic types: those that give orders, warn road users or provide information. Here are ten signs and what they mean, using guidance from the Highway Code and sign maker Hirst Signs. This board tells drivers that another sign is not currently in use, according to Hirst Signs. The company says it may cover a temporary speed limit, a roadworks warning or a diversion that is no longer in place. A sign showing a vehicle and an explosion means vehicles carrying explosives are prohibited. It is a restriction on what the vehicle is carrying, rather than a warning that other cars might explode. This triangular warning sign means slow-moving military vehicles are likely to be in or crossing the road ahead. Hirst Signs says the sign may appear near military bases. A red-bordered sign showing a horse-drawn vehicle means those vehicles are prohibited. It is different from a warning sign telling drivers that horse-drawn vehicles may be on the road. A warning sign with a lightning-shaped symbol alerts road users to an overhead electric cable. The Highway Code says an accompanying plate indicates the maximum height of vehicles that can pass safely. A white circle with a red border means no vehicles, rather than just no motor vehicles. The Highway Code says bicycles can pass if they are being pushed, but not ridden. Check any accompanying plate, which may give times or other qualifications to a restriction. A triangular sign featuring a toad warns drivers of a migratory toad crossing ahead. Hirst Signs says the warning is used where toads cross the road, particularly during breeding season. A triangular sign bearing the word “Ford” warns that the road crosses a stream or river. Water levels can rise in poor weather, so a crossing that is normally shallow may become hazardous. A blue circle with a red border and red cross means no stopping on a clearway. The restriction applies to the main carriageway at any time. A blue circular sign with two white arrows means vehicles may pass on either side to reach the same destination. Unlike a keep-left sign, it allows a choice of which side to use.

metadata.title: Plans for nurse-led care home in Hunts village
metadata.contentSnippet: Plans submitted to turn Little Orchard in Catworth, Huntingdonshire, into a nurse-led care home for six residents, with 24-hour staff and a day centre.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Plans for nurse-led care home in Hunts village
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted to expand a community hub in a Huntingdonshire village into a nurse-led care home. A retrospective application to Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC) seeks to change the use of the property at 41 Station Road in Catworth from a home to a small residential care home and day centre, known as Little Orchard. The care home would provide permanent accommodation for six residents, each with their own room, and communal areas, with nursing staff on duty 24 hours a day. The previous use of the property was a 7-bedroom dwelling with associated parking and garage (class C3), but the plans would see the use change to class C2. The planning statement submitted with the application, from operator Golden Community, said the facility would offer companionship, activities, nutritional support, and nurse-led wellbeing oversight. Golden Community already operates Little Orchard Community Hub which offers day activities, hobbies, social groups, meals, refreshments, health drop-in sessions and support for adults, but hopes to expand into a small care home. On their website, the organisation states: "Our vision is to provide an alternative to a traditional large care-home environment: a small, familiar and homely setting with nursing support, beautiful communal spaces, private rooms and access to the wider Little Orchard community." The plans state that residents would not have private vehicles, and visitor appointments would be staggered to manage traffic. All parking associated with the development would be accommodated within the site, which has nine parking spaces, including four staff spaces, three visitor spaces, one accessible space, and a dedicated ambulance bay. No additional parking spaces are proposed. At least two members of staff would be on duty at all times when the nursing home is operating, with staffing levels increasing if residents' needs become greater. Full details on the planning application are available on the HDC planning portal using reference 26/02108/FUL.

metadata.title: 10 pubs in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Looking for the best place to buy a pint or book a Sunday roast, but don't know where to look? Don't worry, we've got you covered. Let's be honest, when it comes to finding a proper local, we're truly spoilt for choice in Cambridgeshire. So, to help you make up your mind, we've rounded up 10 incredible pubs you have to visit at least once. A multi‑award‑winning riverside pub near the River Great Ouse, known for refined, seasonal cooking and a serious wine list. Regularly recommended in dining guides, it balances white‑tablecloth quality with a relaxed country‑pub atmosphere and a pretty garden that comes into its own in summer. It boasts a rating of 4.3 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 1,250 reviews and 4.5 stars out of 5 on Google. A handsome thatched pub near the Northamptonshire border, The Pheasant majors on polished modern British dishes and an impressive drinks list. Inside you’ll find beams, open fires and an intimate dining room, making it a strong choice for special‑occasion suppers and long Sunday lunches. It boasts a rating of 4.4 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 800 reviews and 4.7 stars out of 5 on Google. Grade II‑listed and set in a picture‑postcard village, The Crown Inn blends flagstone and beams character with creative, seasonal menus. Reviewers highlight its warm welcome, generous roasts and restaurant‑quality food, while the bar still feels like a proper village hub. It boasts a rating of 4.6 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 881 reviews and 4.7 stars out of 5 on Google. Right on the riverside, The Cutter pairs big views of the river with crowd‑pleasing pub favourites and a busy terrace. It’s popular with boaters, walkers and day‑trippers, who rate the relaxed atmosphere, hearty portions and the chance to watch the world go by with a pint. It boasts a rating of 4.3 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 1,250 reviews and 4.5 stars out of 5 on Google. A well‑regarded micropub in Ely’s centre, the Drayman’s Son specialises in cask and craft beer in a compact, sociable space. Expect rotating local brews, knowledgeable staff and a friendly chat-over-pints vibe rather than loud music or big‑screen sport. It boasts a rating of 4.8 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 183 reviews and 4.8 stars out of 5 on Google. Near the riverside, The Acre is praised for its home‑cooked Sunday carvery, friendly service and relaxed, dog‑friendly feel. A pleasant outdoor area makes it a good summer stop‑off, especially for narrowboaters and walkers exploring Fenland waterways. It boasts a rating of 4.4 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off 319 reviews. Overlooking the River Great Ouse, near Littleport, this inn offers riverside drinking, dining and rooms. Visitors highlight welcoming staff, solid pub classics and the appeal of sitting by the water with a drink after a walk or cycle along the river. It boasts a rating of 3.7 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off 74 reviews and 4.3 stars out of 5 on Google. Set by a village green near Oundle, The Chequered Skipper draws strong reviews for its charming setting and quality food. Inside feels country‑cosy, while the green‑side tables are ideal for summer evenings and family gatherings. It boasts a rating of 4.8 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 90 reviews and 4.5 stars out of 5 on Google. A quirky Peterborough fixture, Charters is a real‑ale bar on a converted Dutch barge moored on the Nene. Known for its beer range, live music and relaxed atmosphere, it’s a distinctive spot for riverside drinks close to the city centre. It boasts a rating of 4.1 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 130 reviews and 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google. Tucked in North Street, the historic Ostrich Inn is one of the city’s most characterful pubs. It combines real ale and simple pub dishes with regular live music and events, earning a loyal following among locals and visitors seeking atmosphere over slickness. It boasts a rating of 3.9 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 40 reviews and 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google. Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: CQC recognises significant improvements across East of England Ambulance Service
metadata.contentSnippet: An ambulance service has been rated “Good” after inspectors found major improvements in staffing and patient access.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: CQC recognises significant improvements across East of England Ambulance Service
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An ambulance service has been rated “good” after inspectors found major improvements in staffing and patient access. The East of England Ambulance Service NHS Trust (EEAST) welcomed the Care Quality Commission’s (CQC) latest findings on its Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and Urgent and Emergency Care (UEC) services. Inspectors rated the trust’s EOC “Good” overall and in all five areas assessed: safe, effective, caring, responsive and well-led. Urgent and Emergency Care was also rated “Good” in all five areas, with the CQC praising improvements in safety, responsiveness and leadership. The findings represent a turnaround from the regulator's previous inspection in November 2024, when concerns were raised about staffing levels and how quickly patients could access services. Following that inspection, the CQC served a Section 29A Warning Notice after finding the trust in breach of regulations relating to staffing and safe care and treatment. Inspectors said the service lacked enough staff with the right skills, qualifications and experience, while call waiting times fell below national standards. During the latest inspection, however, the regulator found improvements had been made to call handling and dispatch times and that the EOC was no longer in breach of those regulations. The CQC also found faster ambulance responses in Urgent and Emergency Care and said the service had met the warning notice’s requirements. Inspectors praised progress in staffing, mandatory training, appraisals, safeguarding, call handling, dispatch and ambulance response times. The CQC inspected the trust’s three Emergency Operations Centres in Bedford, Norwich and Chelmsford and spoke to call handlers, dispatchers, clinical co-ordinators and managers. Inspectors also examined six ambulance bases and held seven focus groups as part of their assessment of Urgent and Emergency Care, speaking to around 105 members of staff. They also accompanied ambulance crews responding to urgent calls and reviewed policies and procedures. EEAST provides emergency ambulance services 24 hours a day across Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire, Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, covering around 7,500 square miles and a population of more than 6.2 million people. The CQC did not speak directly to patients because its Emergency Operations Centre inspection had no patient-facing element. Inspectors praised improvements in workforce capacity and performance, including the trust’s Cardiac Arrest Desk initiative. Neill Moloney, chief executive of EEAST, said: "These findings recognise the enormous amount of work colleagues across EEAST have put into improving our services for patients. "The progress reflected in these reports is a testament to their professionalism, commitment and determination to deliver high-quality care every day. "We are proud that the CQC has recognised these improvements." Mr Moloney admitted more work was needed, particularly to make leadership and management consistently effective across Urgent and Emergency Care. He added: "We also recognise the areas of continued focus identified by the CQC, particularly around ensuring leadership and management arrangements are consistently effective across all parts of our Urgent and Emergency Care service, and we remain committed to building on the progress we have made." The earlier Section 29A notice also covered failures in investigating and mitigating controlled-drug incidents, service culture and using staff feedback to improve services.

metadata.title: Aldi trialling changes to some of its UK stores that shoppers might notice
metadata.contentSnippet: Aldi has confirmed it will be trialling changes to some of its UK stores by reducing the number of products it sells.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Aldi trialling changes to some of its UK stores that shoppers might notice
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The budget supermarket Aldi has confirmed it will be making some changes to a range of its UK stores. Aldi hopes the changes will help the store remain efficient and keep prices low compared to other supermarkets. The brand will be trialling reducing the number of products it sells in some of its stores across the UK. The changes come after being “outpaced” by Lidl in its sales growth over the last three years, according to The Grocer. Over the past year, Lidl’s market share has grown from 8.2% to 8.6% with its sales rising by 6.6% year on year. For Aldi, sales have grown by 0.4% year on year with the supermarket’s share dropping from 10.5% to 10.4%. An Aldi spokesperson said: “As a discounter, we’ve always kept things simple so that we can deliver what matters most to our customers – award-winning quality at everyday low prices.” The brand will be making similar changes to its stores in Europe including Switzerland and Germany. Aldi regularly reviews what items it produces and the range of products available in its stores to reflect what customers want. A report from the Competition & Markets Authority (CMA) that was released in August said Aldi’s core grocery range features around 4,000 to 5,000 products when counting different flavours and temporary lines. More than 90% of the products are from Aldi’s own brand. The report said Aldi had understated the size of its grocery range by around 40% with the brand saying it had around 2,000 to 3,000 products. Lidl had similar differences in the number of products it claimed it sold compared to what the report found. Recommended reading Lidl sells a few hundred more products compared to Aldi with around 80% to 90% being from its own label. Aldi’s spokesperson added: “Our volume sales are growing ahead of the market, and we’ve welcomed an additional 140,000 shoppers through our doors in the past 12 weeks as customers recognise that the simple everyday low prices we offer can help them get more value from their weekly shop.” Do you prefer to shop at Aldi or Lidl? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Martin Lewis says £100 energy payment 'won't cover' January bill increase
metadata.contentSnippet: Martin Lewis has warned households to prepare for a huge jump in energy bills after Ofgem confirmed today (November 25) that the price cap will rise by 26% in January.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis says £100 energy payment 'won't cover' January bill increase
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has warned households to prepare for a huge jump in energy bills after Ofgem confirmed today (November 25) that the price cap will rise by 26% in January. The Money Saving Expert founder discussed the looming increase on his television show last night, warning that households could face an extra £160 to £170 in energy costs over just three months. His forecast proved remarkably close to the figure confirmed by regulator Ofgem this morning, with the new price cap set at £2,166 a year for a typical household using gas and electricity and paying by Direct Debit. This is an increase of £443 compared with the current annualised figure of £1,723, and will affect around 20 million households on variable tariffs. The confirmed increase means the price cap will reach its highest level in almost four years , putting further pressure on households already struggling with the cost of living. Martin also warned that the headline 26% increase would not affect every household in the same way, with gas users potentially facing a much bigger jump than electricity-only households. He explained that the increase was being driven primarily by the amount people pay for each unit of energy, rather than standing charges. Speaking on his show, he said: "But this is the really big thing to look at: standing charges not up that much. The unit rates, the amount you pay for each unit of gas and electricity, that is where the big rise is going to come from. "Electricity up 24%, gas up 37%." Tomorrow morning, Ofgem will announce the Jan-March energy price cap. It's likely to go up 26% but what after that? And does this mean you should fix? A clip from my Martin Lewis Money Show energy special tonight. Watch the full thing for far more help: https://t.co/Vcrj5Jywiw https://t.co/yR2mlzgyBw — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 24, 2026 The warning also comes after Chancellor John Healey announced a one-off £100 Household Energy Payment for around 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. The money is expected to start reaching eligible households in January 2027, but Martin warned it would not be enough to offset the increase in energy costs for most people. He said: "That is a rise of £160 to £170 just from January to the end of March, not 2027. Just January to the end of March. "The government energy support of £100 is paid in January for those in council tax bands A to D, it will not cover the rise for most households." The Government's £100 payment will therefore provide some help, but households could still face a significant shortfall. Martin also used last night's programme to examine whether households should consider moving away from their current variable energy tariff and locking into a fixed deal - but explained that every situation is different. He warned that energy prices could remain substantially higher throughout 2027, although he stressed that forecasts further into the year were much less certain. He said: "If those predictions are right, and this is pretty certain, it is going to be substantially higher throughout 2027 than it is now." Martin then highlighted the cheapest two-year fixed deal available at the time of his programme, which was around 2% more expensive than the existing price cap. That means customers choosing the deal would initially pay slightly more over the remaining weeks of the current price cap period. However, if the January forecasts proved correct, he said they could save more than 20% between January and March, with potentially further savings over the following year - but while it is good to consider options, circumstances will vary. Recommended reading : He was careful not to guarantee that switching would save money, saying: "I cannot tell you that fixing will save you money because I would need a crystal ball, but I can tell you the vast balance of probabilities means it will save you money over the next year." He added: "And if you are risk averse and want to avoid those January price hikes, fixing is the sensible option if you are on the price cap." As always, households should compare available tariffs against their own energy usage and check any exit fees before switching, as the cheapest deal will vary depending on where they live and how much energy they use.

metadata.title: Woman found dead in Cambridgeshire named amid murder investigation
metadata.contentSnippet: A woman found dead in Wisbech has been named amid a police murder investigation which saw a man arrested.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Woman found dead in Cambridgeshire named amid murder investigation
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman found dead in a Cambridgeshire town has been named amid a police murder investigation. The force were called to Alexandra Road in Wisbech at around 9.50pm on Saturday, November 21, to reports a 61-year-old woman's body was discovered at a property. She has now been named as Vera Jaunzeme. A 62-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and taken to hospital, where he remains. Police and specialist scenes of crime officers are at the scene and investigations are ongoing. Detective Inspector Andrew Moralee, from the Major Crime Unit, said the death is being treated as an isolated incident. He said: "Our thoughts are with Vera’s family and friends at this very difficult time." A post-mortem examination is due to take place on November 26. Anyone with information is asked to contact police online or call 101, quoting Op Emeth.

metadata.title: Confirmation that 'debacle' car park scheme will not progress welcomed
metadata.contentSnippet: Confirmation that a 'shambolic' scheme to build housing developments on St Neots, St Ives and Huntingdon car parks will not be progressed has been welcomed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Confirmation that 'debacle' car park scheme will not progress welcomed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Confirmation that a 'shambolic' scheme to build housing developments on car parks will not be progressed has been welcomed in Huntingdonshire. Proposals to transform Tebbutts Road car park in St Neots, Princes Street car park in Huntingdon and the old cattle market in St Ives into developments with up to 80 homes were first unveiled to the public in August. The plans were put forward by property developer Capital & Centric in partnership with Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC). The news sparked fury among residents concerned over the potential loss of parking spaces in the town centres. After a series of public consultations and around 90% of residents who were asked opposing the scheme, it was revealed that the developments were "highly unlikely" to go ahead. The St Neots public consultation in August (Image: Emily Stevens) At an extraordinary cabinet meeting of HDC at Pathfinder House on November 24, councillors assured the public that they will no be progressing the regeneration projects in their current form beyond Gateway 1. Cllr Ross Martin was first to speak, calling the scheme a "debacle" and "shambolic". He also called for a clear decision to be made that evening to reassure residents, despite it not technically being needed. The way the council operates means the scheme naturally comes to a close after Gateway 1 and a decision is needed to progress to Gateway 2, as there is no automatic commitment to do so. Cllr Liam Dewey-Beckett said: "We are not going any further with these schemes." Council leader Cllr Sarah Conboy also assured the public the project would not be moving forward. An independent review on the funding for the Capital & Centric projects will continue to be conducted, as HDC voted to review the funds after £1m was spent. The news that the plans will not progress has been welcomed by the Huntingdon Business Improvement District (BID). Paul Sweeney, chief executive officer of BID Huntingdon First, said: "The last few months have been incredibly difficult to navigate both personally as a resident of Huntingdon and professionally as the CEO of the Business Improvement District representing 300 businesses in Huntingdon town centre. "However last night’s decision at the cabinet meeting, which I attended in person, puts a welcome end to months of uncertainty for many."

metadata.title: FOWL Community Event
Cold Weather Payment of £25 a week to help thousands with winter heating bills
metadata.contentSnippet: Households could receive extra financial help this winter as the DWP prepares to make Cold Weather Payments worth £25 during periods of freezing temperatures.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cold Weather Payment of £25 a week to help thousands with winter heating bills
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of households could receive extra financial help this winter as the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) prepares to make Cold Weather Payments worth £25 during periods of freezing temperatures. The payments are designed to help people on certain benefits cope with the additional costs of keeping warm when temperatures plummet. Eligible households will receive £25 for every seven-day period when the average temperature in their area is recorded as, or forecast to be, zero degrees Celsius or below. The scheme runs from November 1, 2026, until March 31, 2027, meaning households could receive multiple payments if freezing conditions persist. Importantly, the money is paid automatically, so eligible people do not need to make a claim. However, some households may need to tell the DWP about changes in their circumstances to make sure they do not miss out. The DWP says people receiving certain benefits may qualify for Cold Weather Payments. These include: However, simply receiving one of these benefits does not necessarily mean you will qualify. There are additional conditions depending on the benefit you claim. People receiving Pension Credit will usually qualify for Cold Weather Payments. This is particularly important for older households struggling with heating costs during the winter months. Pension Credit is a means-tested benefit designed to top up the income of people over State Pension age. People receiving Universal Credit can usually qualify if they, and their partner if they have one, are not employed or gainfully self-employed. They must also meet at least one of the following conditions: Households with a disabled child amount included in their Universal Credit claim will also qualify, regardless of whether either adult is working or self-employed. People claiming income-related Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) will usually qualify if they are in the work-related activity group or support group. Those outside these groups may still be eligible if they receive certain additional premiums or have particular caring responsibilities. These include: People receiving Support for Mortgage Interest (SMI) may also qualify, provided they are treated as receiving a qualifying benefit and meet certain additional conditions. These include having a severe or enhanced disability premium, a pensioner premium, a disabled child or a child under five living in the household. The DWP says people can sometimes be treated as receiving a qualifying benefit even if they do not actually receive it because their income is too high. Some households may need to take action to make sure they receive the money. People claiming Universal Credit or income-related ESA must report a change in circumstances if they have a baby or a child under five comes to live with them. This is important because the DWP will not automatically know about these changes. Universal Credit claimants should report the change through their online account or contact the Universal Credit helpline. People receiving income-related ESA should tell Jobcentre Plus. Failing to report the change could mean missing out on payments they would otherwise qualify for. We're closing a loophole in Universal Credit Serious offenders detained for hospital treatment will no longer receive benefits while their living costs are being met by the NHS Watch Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden discuss the changes on @GMB https://t.co/ibm9VjDQ1w — Department for Work and Pensions (@DWPgovuk) October 20, 2026 Cold Weather Payments are triggered when the average temperature in an eligible area is recorded as, or forecast to be, zero degrees Celsius or below for seven consecutive days. For every qualifying seven-day period between November 1, 2026, and March 31, 2027, eligible households will receive £25. The money should arrive within 14 working days of the qualifying cold weather period. It will be paid directly into the same bank or building society account used for existing benefit payments. There is no need to apply or contact the DWP to trigger the payment if you already meet the eligibility requirements. Households in England and Wales can use the Government's online Cold Weather Payment checker to see whether their postcode has experienced a qualifying period of cold weather. The checker is available here . People living in Northern Ireland can use a separate postcode checker through nidirect. If someone believes they should have received a payment but has not, they should contact the Pension Service or Jobcentre Plus. Universal Credit claimants can instead add a note to their online journal or contact the Universal Credit helpline. Pensioners with income up to the value of the full new state pension (to be £13,040 from April 2027) will not pay tax. Mechanism not stated, I suspect there will be an effective increased pensioner allowance with a clawback for income above that. More when I know more. #Budget2026 — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) October 28, 2026 It is important not to confuse Cold Weather Payments with Winter Fuel Payments. Cold Weather Payments are triggered by freezing temperatures and are worth £25 for each qualifying seven-day period. Winter Fuel Payments are a separate annual payment designed to help eligible pensioners with heating bills. The two schemes have different eligibility rules and payment arrangements. Recommended reading: People living in Scotland cannot receive Cold Weather Payments. Instead, they may qualify for the annual Winter Heating Payment. Unlike Cold Weather Payments, this is paid regardless of how cold the weather gets in the recipient's area.

metadata.title: Martin Lewis on cheapest fixes available now as energy bills to rocket in January
metadata.contentSnippet: Martin Lewis has issued an urgent warning to anyone still on a standard variable tariff as the Energy Price Cap shoots up in January

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis on cheapest fixes available now as energy bills to rocket in January
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of households face a sharp rise in energy bills from January, prompting consumer champion Martin Lewis to issue an urgent warning to anyone still on a standard variable tariff. The founder of MoneySavingExpert says customers who have not fixed their energy prices could see bills soar when the new Energy Price Cap takes effect on January 1. And with energy experts warning prices could remain elevated for the rest of 2027, Martin Lewis says now could be one of the last opportunities to secure a cheaper fixed deal before rates climb further. Martin Lewis said: "If you're on your firm's standard variable tariff, get off it." He's shared some of the lowest deals still available on his Money Saving Expert site, but advises everyone to do a full market price comparison to get their own best deal - depending on their usage and circumstances. Alongside switching tariffs, financial experts say households can cut bills further through a few simple changes. Aseem Munshi, founder of Updraft, estimates households could save up to £433 a year by: Televisions, chargers, gaming consoles and kitchen appliances can continue drawing power even when switched off. Munshi says eliminating this standby usage could save up to £147 annually. A typical 10-minute electric shower can cost hundreds of pounds over a year. Reducing shower time from 10 minutes to three minutes could save around £186 a year. Cooking multiple meals at once and reheating them later can significantly reduce oven usage. Munshi estimates households could save around £100 a year through meal prepping and batch cooking. Recommended reading: Experts say the decision depends on your current tariff. If you're on: Martin Lewis says those most concerned about future price rises may prefer the certainty of fixing now, while households willing to take more risk could wait to see whether wholesale prices continue to fall. But with the Energy Price Cap set to jump, experts agree that doing nothing could prove the most expensive option of all.

metadata.title: Ryanair quietly makes major change to seating policy affecting all passengers
metadata.contentSnippet: Ryanair passengers choosing free random seats will now learn their allocation just over three hours before departure, after a quiet booking system change.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ryanair quietly makes major change to seating policy affecting all passengers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major change to Ryanair's booking system means passengers will now be assigned free seats just three hours before departure. Previously, travellers using the 'free' seat option could see their assigned seat 24 hours before their flight. The low-cost carrier confirmed that the update quietly took effect at the end of October. A Ryanair spokesperson said: "The timing of the allocation of free random seats is determined at all times by the airline. "We moved this allocation from 24 hours to over three hours (prior to departure) when we cut across to our winter schedule at the end of Oct last. "The reason for this time change is to allow those passengers who wish to select their preferred seat more time to do so. "We had a number of complaints this summer that passengers could not book their preferred seat on the day of travel as it had been already randomly allocated as a free seat up to 24 hours prior to departure. "Passengers who choose a free of charge random seat clearly don’t mind where they sit, and their digital boarding pass is automatically updated between three to four hours prior to departure, which is well before they arrive at either their departure airport or their boarding gate." Under the previous system, passengers were given the chance to upgrade, which would involve paying for a seat of their choice. Now, passengers wanting to guarantee a seat choice—such as an aisle or window—must pay to select it, or take their chances with a randomly assigned seat closer to departure. The change means those who opt not to pay will only find out where they are seated a few hours before their flight, instead of the day before. What do you think of the policy change? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

metadata.title: DWP Winter Fuel Payments start landing – full list of who gets £100, £200 or £300
metadata.contentSnippet: Millions of pensioners are due Winter Fuel Payments for 2026/27. See the full eligibility rules, payment rates and £35,000 HMRC threshold.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP Winter Fuel Payments start landing – full list of who gets £100, £200 or £300
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is starting to pay out this year's Winter Fuel Payment, with millions of older people due to receive a one-off cash boost to help with heating bills. The annual payment is designed to help pensioners manage higher energy costs during the colder months, with eligible households receiving between £100 and £300 for winter 2026/27. People who qualify should have received a letter in October or November confirming how much they are due to receive. Most payments are made automatically, meaning pensioners do not need to make a claim. However, some people may need to contact the DWP if they believe they qualify but have not received a letter. To qualify for the Winter Fuel Payment this year, you must have been born on or before June 27, 1960, and usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. The amount you receive depends on your age, who you live with and whether you or someone in your household claims certain benefits. You can qualify for the Winter Fuel Payment if you: However, there are some circumstances where you will not qualify. You will not be eligible if you: People living in care homes can still qualify, but will not be eligible if they receive Universal Credit, Pension Credit or income-related Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) and have lived in a care home throughout the period since June 29, 2026. The amount you receive depends on your date of birth and your living arrangements during the qualifying week of September 21 to 27, 2026. If you live alone, or nobody else in your household qualifies for the Winter Fuel Payment, you will receive: If you live with someone else who also qualifies and neither of you receives certain means-tested benefits, the payment is: If you and your partner jointly claim Pension Credit, Universal Credit or income-related ESA, one of you will receive: If you receive one of these benefits but are not part of a joint claim, you will receive £200 or £300 depending on your date of birth. People living in care homes who qualify will receive £100 if born between September 28, 1946, and June 27, 1960, or £150 if born before September 28, 1946. Most eligible pensioners will receive their Winter Fuel Payment automatically in November or December 2026. The money will normally be paid into the same bank or building society account used for your State Pension or other benefits. You should have received a letter in October or November explaining how much you will get. If you believe you qualify but have not received a letter, you should check whether you need to make a claim through the Government's Winter Fuel Payment service. Any money you receive will not affect your other benefits. Pensioners with an individual income of more than £35,000 will have their Winter Fuel Payment reclaimed by HMRC. This means eligible people can still receive the money, but it will subsequently be taken back through the tax system. Recommended reading: HMRC will recover the payment either by changing your tax code or adding the amount to your Self Assessment tax return. Importantly, the £35,000 threshold applies to your own income, not your household income. Your partner's earnings do not count towards it. People living in Scotland cannot receive the DWP Winter Fuel Payment. Instead, eligible older people may qualify for the Scottish Government's Pension Age Winter Heating Payment, which provides separate support towards heating costs.

metadata.title: Crews rush to 'deliberate' fire at former RAF base in Hunts village
metadata.contentSnippet: Firefighters rushed to a "deliberate" fire at the derelict former RAF Upwood base on Ramsey Road in Bury on November 21, 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Crews rush to 'deliberate' fire at former RAF base in Hunts village
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Firefighters rushed to a "deliberate" fire at a derelict former RAF base in a Huntingdonshire village. Crews were called to the former RAF Upwood site on Ramsey Road near Bury on Saturday, November 21, at 3.31pm. The base opened in 1917 after a nearby farm was requisitioned for use as an emergency landing ground. Standing mostly derelict since 1994, the site has been the target of fly tipping and arson attacks for a number of years. However, there have been plans to redevelop areas into community facilities. Crews from Ramsey arrived to find a blaze on the ground floor of the derelict building and used a hose reel to extinguish it. They returned to the station by 4.10pm. A statement from Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service reads: "The cause of the fire is believed to be deliberate." Anyone with information should contact Cambridgeshire Police via their website, quoting incident 445 of November 21. Alternatively, call Crimestoppers on 0800 555111.

metadata.title: St Ives wine bar allowed to open later after ‘error’ in earlier application
metadata.contentSnippet: St Ives wine bar Broadway Cellars can open later after a planning error, with Huntingdonshire District Council approving extended Sunday and weekday hours.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ives wine bar allowed to open later after ‘error’ in earlier application
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A wine bar has been given permission to open later on Sundays and weekdays after an “error” was made on an earlier application. Broadway Cellars opened in St Ives late last year and has since become a popular destination in the historic market town. The bar applied to Huntingdonshire District Council to extend its opening hours until midnight on Thursdays and 1am on Fridays and Saturdays, which was approved. The business at 34 The Broadway previously had to close at 11pm from Wednesday to Saturday and also applied to host live music on Fridays and Saturdays. But a further application was made after an error in the application meant the bar was still limited to closing at 7pm on Mondays, Tuesdays and Sundays. The bar had sought to extend this until 11pm on Mondays and Tuesdays and midnight on Wednesdays and Sundays. A report from HDC’s planning officers said they “understand there was an error with the earlier submission” and “so a further amendment to the opening hours is being sought under this application”. Despite having a licence to open later, a condition on the planning application meant the bar was unable to do so. St Ives Town Council supported the extension they said “would be consistent” with “other pubs in the area” and “acknowledged the success of Broadway Cellars”. The combined bar and wine shop offers not just a wide range of wine to purchase but also cocktails and beers. As a condition of their licence a CCTV system has to be installed and maintained with recordings kept for 31 consecutive days.

metadata.title: Discover 'gorgeous' street food haven dubbed 'coolest place'
metadata.contentSnippet: A family friendly venue with coffee shop, restaurant and bar all rolled into one has been hailed the "coolest place" in Ely by visitors.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Discover 'gorgeous' street food haven dubbed 'coolest place'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A family friendly venue with coffee shop, restaurant and bar all rolled into one has been hailed the "coolest place" by visitors. The Yard is tucked away on Newnham Street, in Ely, and was described as the city's "latest treat" when it opened. Silver Oak Coffee, Ely's independent coffee roastery owned by Susanne Stent and Bruce Garside, opened the venue in March 2023. It is described as a "proper independent venue" (Image: The Yard) More than 600 guests poured into the "gorgeous" new venue when it opened, which is spread over five shipping containers. It features a children’s play area, coffee shop, restaurant, bar and outdoor seating area and was designed as a space that "brings people together". On its website, The Yard proudly describes itself as a "proper independent venue run by people who care about every detail, from the playlist to the pour". Naturally, The Yard has received dozens of raving reviews on Trip Advisor, with more than 50 rating the venue as "excellent" One visitor said: "The Yard feels like one of those places that instantly lifts the mood — informal, creative, and full of life." The Yard serves "seasonal, locally-sourced food that goes way beyond standard pub grub" and boasts a bar team of "cocktail nerds" and "whiskey geeks". The Yard opened its doors in March 2023 (Image: The Yard) "Community is at the heart of everything we do. We support local artists, musicians, and suppliers. "We host art exhibitions, give platforms to emerging talent, and try to make sure that every person who walks through our doors feels like they belong." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: The award-winning steakhouse dubbed 'heaven' for beer lovers
metadata.contentSnippet: Visitors can't get enough of an award-winning steakhouse in Cambridgeshire dubbed a "heaven" for beer lovers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The award-winning steakhouse dubbed 'heaven' for beer lovers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Visitors can't get enough of an award-winning steakhouse in Cambridgeshire dubbed a "heaven" for beer lovers. Tucked away on High Street Passage, in Ely, Griddle Bar and Meat House has been described as an "unforgettable dining experience". The venue opened its doors "to a great hoorah" in November 2024 and owner Juliana Hunt believes the meat on offer is the best in the county. The restaurant first opened in November 2024 (Image: Griddle Bar and Meat House) On its website, the restaurant proudly describes itself as being "dedicated to serving the finest quality steaks and handcrafted beers". As well as the "finest selection of premium meats", a range of "tastebud-challenging" beers are on offer, including the Slippery Elly and Sniggler's Hat. Griddle Bar and Meat House has racked up raving reviews, with visitors praising it "great food" and "beautiful" craft beer. One visitor said: "I recently tried the craft beer at Griddle Bar and Meat House. It poured a beautiful, hazy golden with a white head. "The aroma was immediately, citrus-forward with hints of passionfruit. Overall, a great addition to their menu." Another said: "Great Food, great atmosphere, and excellent service. The steaks were cooked perfectly and full of flavour. "One of my favourite spots in Ely! Great craft beer selection. Highly recommended." The venue is a hit with visitors (Image: Griddle Bar and Meat House) The independent steakhouse serves breakfast, lunch and dinner and is "perfect for date nights, family meals and gatherings with friends". It's menu is built around "quality local ingredients" ranging from "artisan breads and local sources coffee to prime cuts of meat". Just last year, its burgers were ranked among the best in Cambridgeshire by Cambridge Foodies. "If you haven't tried our burgers, we have got everything you need to satisfy those cravings," a spokesperson said. The Axe and Compass, in Hemingford Abbots, promises a "beautiful beer garden" and an al-fresco dining area. On its website, the venue, which dates back to the 15th century, describes how "there is something for everyone". Set against the background of the village church spire, the "picturesque " pub is run by Emma and Stuart Tester. The couple have been a part of the pub for more than 25-years and now run the business together while also holding down full-time jobs. Serving a range of classics as well as offering a Sunday menu, the pair are "very passionate about serving good quality homemade dishes". The Axe and Compass also boasts outside catering, including buffets, hog roasts and BBQs as well as regular music nights and other events. Featuring a country snug and wood burning stoves, it shouldn't come as much surprise the venue has received a number of excellent reviews on Trip Advisor. One visitor said: "Honestly we have lived in the village for five years but always skipped over the pub. "I can say with confidence that after todays meal we wont any more. The food was absolutely lovely with a bustling Friday evening environment." Another added: "A group of 22 of us enjoyed lunch here. We pre-ordered and everything was served shortly after we arrived. "Everyone enjoyed their meal and the service was attentive and friendly." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk or newsdesk@huntspost.co.uk

metadata.title: Discover 'lovely' nature reserve in Cambridgeshire with 'beautiful walks'
metadata.contentSnippet: Love exploring green spaces and fancy a nice walk? Then this much-loved nature reserve in Cambridgeshire is for you.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Discover 'lovely' nature reserve in Cambridgeshire with 'beautiful walks'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Love exploring green spaces and fancy a nice walk? Then this much-loved nature reserve in Cambridgeshire is for you. Described as a "lovely gem", nature lovers can't help but rave about Paxton Pits Nature Reserve. A tranquil wildlife haven nestled in Little Paxton, the reserve has earned glowing praise from visitors for its peaceful atmosphere, scenic beauty and diverse wildlife. On TripAdvisor, the reserve has more than 150 'excellent' reviews, with visitors recommending it as a must visit for families and nature lovers. Elsewhere, on Google Reviews, Paxton Pits has a score of 4.7 out of 5 from more than 99 reviews. Covering 77 hectares, the reserve features a variety of habitats, including lakes, meadow, grassland, scrub, and woodland. It is managed by Huntingdonshire District Council in partnership with the Friends of Paxton Pits. Just last year, Paxton Pits Nature Reserve was a recipient of the coveted Green Flag Award. Recognising the best parks and green spaces internationally, the scheme provides the high standards against which sites are measured. Designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) for its populations of water birds, the reserve is particularly popular among birdwatchers. Its also well-known for its nightingales which "can be heard signing between the end of April and June." The range of birds, insects, mammals and flora is "one of the many reasons why Paxton Pits is such a special place", its website says. Each year between the end of April and June, visitors can hear the distinctive song of nightingales. The reserve also includes its very own visitor centre which houses a "great café" serving refreshments and other products. Unsurprisingly, it has received a tidal wave of rave reviews over the years, with visitors praising its "beautiful surroundings". One said: "We had a lovely walk around the site and then stopped for a hot chocolate and a muffin. The staff were lovely and everything was clean and tidy." Another added: "A lovely gem of a place, beautiful walks, amazing scenery, great café, clean, well organised and a great place to spend the day. We went on two different walks and really enjoyed them both." Paxton Pits Nature Reserve is just off the A1, making it a convenient stop for travellers and locals alike. What's your favourite walk in Cambridgeshire? Let us know in the comments. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: 10 Cambridgeshire criminals who were jailed in November
metadata.contentSnippet: Criminals jailed in Cambridgeshire in November 2026 include a serial shoplifter, gang members who supplied cocaine and a controlling partner.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 Cambridgeshire criminals who were jailed in November
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Here are some of the criminals who ended up behind bars across Cambridgeshire in November, including a serial shoplifter, gang members who supplied Cambridgeshire with cocaine and a controlling partner who subjected his victim to a decade of abuse. A serial shoplifter was jailed after targeting the same Fenland shop three days in a row. On August 30, Kallum Payne, 24, of Gaul Road, March, began a spree of thefts at the Superdrug store on Broad Street in March. He stole skincare products with a total value of £457.84 on three consecutive days without attempting to pay. On Tuesday, November 3, at Cambridge Crown Court, Payne was jailed for 18 months, having admitted five counts of theft from a shop. Kallum Payne stole skincare products valued at more than £400 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A second robber was jailed for more than four years for attacking a group of boys in Peterborough and stealing a bicycle. Imran Ali, 41, was jailed for 50 months at Cambridge Crown Court on November 2. The sentence comes after he was found guilty of robbery and two counts of attempted robbery. Together with Declan Hyland, 29, and another man they ambushed the youngsters at around 5pm on April 18. Imran Ali was found guilty of robbery (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A convicted Cambridgeshire sex offender was jailed for breaching a court order after creating a secret social media account. Harry Yeardsley, 20, admitted two breaches of a Sexual Harm Prevention Order (SHPO). The order was imposed earlier this year after Yeardsley pleaded guilty to sexual communication with a child. Officers discovered that Yeardsley had created, used, and deleted an account on Kik. He was jailed for six months at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on November 6. Yousif Nechirvan, 31, and Aras Abrahim, 35, were arrested on February 17 following four simultaneous police warrants at properties in Peterborough. They found 30 wraps of cocaine worth up to £900 concealed in a cigarette packet and £6,000 in cash hidden behind kitchen kickboards. Nechirvan, of Western Avenue, was jailed for three years and seven months and Abrahim, of Whalley Street, was jailed for 28 months. Yousif Nechirvan (left) and Aras Abrahim (right) (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A burglar who "repeatedly targeted" Cambridgeshire properties and stole more than £2,000 worth of alcohol was jailed. Darren Valentine, 35, of no fixed address, admitted three burglaries, five attempted burglaries, breaching a Criminal Behaviour Order and attempting to steal a car. On May 26, Valentine climbed into the rear garden of Margaret’s Cambridge on Chesterton Road and stole £400 worth of alcohol from its cellar. On August 29, he broke into a garage on Mariners Way in Chesterton and stole two bikes, an electric moped and £1,830 worth of alcohol. Valentine was jailed for 20 months at Peterborough Crown Court on November 5. Darren Valentine stole £2,000 worth of alcohol (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A controlling partner who subjected his victim to a decade of abuse and even strangled her was jailed for more than two years. Anthony Bernard, 49, of Croyland Road, Walton, Peterborough, pleaded guilty to engaging in controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship and intentional strangulation. His abuse came to light after an incident on August 11, when he emptied his partner’s wardrobe, took her belongings, and threatened to burn them in a car. Police uncovered more than a decade of coercive and controlling behaviour during their investigation. Bernard was jailed for two years and three months and given a restraining order at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, November 4. Anthony Bernard strangled his victim in a decade of abuse (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A shoplifter was jailed after breaching a court order and going on a three-day stealing spree. Joshua Preece, 21, was sentenced to eight months at Huntingdon Magistrates’ Court on November 12 after admitting four counts of theft from a shop and two breaches of a criminal behaviour order (CBO). The thefts took place in Peterborough between October 30 and November 1, targeting M&S and Next at Brotherhood Retail Park and a BP filling station in Bretton. He also breached his two-year CBO by entering the Bretton Centre on October 26 and 31. Joshua Preece breached a court order (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A shoplifter was jailed after threatening to stab staff with a drill bit at a Peterborough toy shop. Stephen Foot, 29, was confronted by staff at Smyths Toys in Boongate on November 3 when he was caught stealing a toy truck. He pulled out a pointed drill bit and threatened to stab staff if they approached him before fleeing the scene with the stolen item. At Peterborough Magistrates' Court on November 4, he was charged with possession of a bladed article and three counts of theft from a shop and sentenced to six months in prison. A man who stole an orangutan statue priced at more than £700 from a garden centre in Cambridgeshire was jailed for nearly two years. Derek Lundgren, 61, of New Road, Sawston, took the £799 statue from Scotsdales Garden Centre in Horningsea on September 7. He was captured on CCTV leaving the store without paying before jumping on his bike, placing the giant animal figure across the handlebars and cycling off. Lundgren was sentenced to a year and 11 months in prison (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) At Ipswich Magistrates’ Court on November 9, Lundgren was sentenced to a year and 11 months in prison.

metadata.title: Prominence regime risks your right to choose your news
metadata.contentSnippet: Would you prefer to choose the news and information you consume, or would you rather the Government decides for you?

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Prominence regime risks your right to choose your news
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Would you prefer to choose the news and information you consume, or would you rather the Government decides for you? The former allows you to exercise personal choice, judgement and agency. The latter would see the Government trying to take that freedom away and instead serve you news and information it has deemed suitable, relevant and appropriate. It’s confusing and deeply worrying, then, that the latter is what the Government’s proposed prominence regime is looking to do by giving the state a say over which sources of news are pushed up your social media feed, rather than leaving that choice to you. To me, that’s not the sort of edict we would expect in a world-leading democracy like ours, and certainly not in one led by a Prime Minister that has himself recently espoused the value of a free press. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy (Image: Maja Smiejkowska) Journalists are here to represent your interests and hold power to account on your behalf. Often, that means challenging authority in ways that may be uncomfortable or, at times, disruptive to what Government – local, regional or national – is seeking to achieve. So, we must resist any attempt by Government to control our free press. Any influence of Government over what journalists can publish is an erosion of this fundamental principle. This can happen in all sorts of ways. Not all erosion of free speech is an obvious, brutal clampdown. But when we see it in any form, we must act. Earlier this year, Ministers brought forward proposals to make what it describes as trusted sources of news more prominent on social media, in a bid to crack down on mis and disinformation which blights our online ecosystem. On the face of it, a worthy objective. But dig a little deeper and the proposals carry serious and fundamental risks. Firstly, selection of titles for prominence. Who would decide which titles are more prominent online and on what criteria? This matters enormously because deciding which titles receive greater prominence means deciding which sources get an advantage in reaching you, the reader. And whoever is making those decisions suddenly wields massive power and control of the information being read by millions of people every single day. This must not happen. No one should have that kind of power and most certainly not the Government - it’s for you the reader to decide what sources of news you consume, and that must not change. We don’t believe this Government intends to implement draconian censorship, but the power it is intending to give itself over the dissemination of news and topical information could easily be weaponised by future administrations with more nefarious and dangerous objectives. That is a dystopian nightmare. It could also narrow the range of news you see. Ranking is a zero-sum game: every title pushed up your feed pushes another down. A plural press depends on readers drawing on many different sources, but prominence would push in the opposite direction. The other big question here is how, from a technical and practical perspective, a prominence regime could possibly work for local news publishers serving hundreds of communities across the UK. I’m not sure, and I’m pretty sure the Government doesn’t know either. The obvious answer for such a regime is that it would have to involve highly invasive tracking of users with hundreds if not thousands of individual regulatory regimes running in parallel across the country. Otherwise, how could local news get to local people in areas where titles overlap? The regime would also disproportionately benefit the BBC, the UK’s publicly funded broadcaster. Let’s remember, the BBC is already hell bent on using its own licence-fee funded digital local news services to squash commercial local news providers. And, in reality, the tech platforms this regime relies on would just give prominence to the BBC because, on a technical level, it’s easier and why would they give themselves an undue headache? Some will say prominence is a way to take on the tech giants. But it would leave their grip on news firmly in place. The platforms would still own the algorithms, still decide how to comply, still surface mis- and disinformation - and still keep most of the value of the journalism that passes through their feeds. All the regime would add is the hand of the state on top. We are being offered a choice between platform power and state power. It is a false choice. Power should instead move to the people this is supposed to be about: you, the reader, and the publishers who produce the journalism you rely on. There is a better way. That means giving you the right to choose which news sources you see more of, and requiring the platforms to respect that choice. It means giving publishers transparency over how platforms rank their journalism and who it reaches, control over how it is presented, so they can build direct relationships with their audiences. And it means backing the Competition and Markets Authority in using its new digital markets powers to make sure the platforms pay fairly for the news they profit from, so publishers can sustain the journalism that keeps communities informed. Alongside that, the Government can make good on its promises to help local journalism thrive by diverting a greater share of central Government advertising to local news titles and keeping public notices in local news media. But prominence is not the right way forward. We have voiced our concerns but need your help to make our case. Contact your local MP today and be clear that you want to continue to choose your news. Theo Bamber, News Media Association Chief Executive

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Passengers are being warned to expect significant disruption to rail services, which could last until this afternoon. All lines between Peterborough and Huntingdon are currently blocked this morning (Tuesday, November 24) due to reports of a broken rail. National Rail confirmed repairs are being carried out following a report of a "possible fault in the area". A spokesperson said: "As a precaution, trains are travelling at reduced speeds through the affected area until the track has been checked. "These speed restrictions allow trains to continue running safely while the issue is investigated. They added: "Some services may also need to be cancelled or changed to prevent delays from spreading across the wider network.
